course.description: Want to finally feel at home with React? We start from JavaScript basics and climb all the way to a portfolio project. Six phases, at your pace, with practice from the first module.

phases.title: What is React, really?
phases.label: Introduction
phases.summary: Before writing a single line of code, let's take a moment to understand what React actually is, why it was created, and why it became essential.

modules.title: A plain definition, no jargon
modules.subtitle: Understand React in one sentence — then really understand it

contentBlocks.html: React is a JavaScript library created by Facebook (now Meta) in 2013 for building user interfaces. That's it. No magic, no mystery: React is a tool that helps you render buttons, forms, lists, whole pages — in short, everything the user sees and interacts with in a browser.
But that definition, while accurate, doesn't say why React became the worldwide standard for modern web development. To get that, you need to go back to the problem it solves.

box.title: An analogy to get started
box.body: Imagine you're building a house. Without React, you make every brick, window, and door by hand, one by one. With React, you design a window model and a door model once, then reuse them as many times as you need. Better still: when you change the paint, React repaints only the walls that need it.

contentBlocks.html: Before React, building an interactive UI with vanilla JavaScript or jQuery was exhausting. On every click, every keystroke, you had to manually:
Find the right HTML element on the page (document.querySelector)
Change its content or style by hand
Sync every part of the UI that depends on that change
Debug for hours when some state was stale somewhere

The bigger the app got, the more the code looked like spaghetti. React offers a radically different idea: describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and let React update the DOM. You move from imperative logic ("do this, then that") to declarative logic ("here's what I want to see").

modules.title: Library or framework? The nuance that changes everything
modules.subtitle: Why React is deliberately minimal — and what that implies

contentBlocks.html: A vocabulary detail that matters: React is a library, not a framework. The difference is philosophical: a framework imposes a structure and calls your code. A library waits for you to call it when you need it.

box.title: Practical consequence
box.body: React only handles the view. For everything else (routing, HTTP requests, global state, complex forms, tests…), you pick the complementary tools yourself. That is both React's greatest strength and its greatest difficulty.

contentBlocks.html: In practice, a modern React stack often looks like: React (view) + React Router (navigation) + TanStack Query (server data) + Zustand (global state) + Tailwind CSS (styles).

modules.title: The 3 fundamental ideas of React
modules.subtitle: If you remember only one thing from this intro, remember these three concepts

contentBlocks.html: All of React's magic rests on three pillars. Everything else — hooks, state, props, effects — is just a set of tools to put those three ideas into practice.

A component is a reusable piece of UI, wrapped in a JavaScript function. A button, a navbar, a page — everything is a component. Like LEGO bricks, components nest to form complex interfaces from simple pieces.

box.title: The promise of components
box.body: You write a Button component once and reuse it in 50 places. The day you change its design, every button updates automatically. No more copy-paste.

contentBlocks.html: As soon as you need to react to an action (a click, a keystroke, a network request), you need memory to track what changes: state. When state changes, React automatically re-draws the affected parts.
The user clicks « Like » → the likes state goes from 3 to 4
React detects the change → recalculates the affected part
The browser shows « 4 likes » — you didn't have to do anything

contentBlocks.text: 3. The Virtual DOM: performance through cleverness

contentBlocks.html: Updating the DOM is slow. React keeps a lightweight copy of the DOM in memory (the Virtual DOM). On every change, it compares the old and new versions, then applies to the real DOM only the differences.

box.title: Prerequisites: This module assumes you know
box.body: Basic HTML/CSS (tags, attributes), JavaScript ES6+ (arrow functions, destructuring, const/let, import/export modules). If any of these foundations feel shaky, revisit them before continuing: React amplifies JS gaps; it does not hide them.

contentBlocks.html: Before React, manually manipulating the DOM with jQuery or Vanilla JS quickly turned into spaghetti code as soon as the interface grew complex. React solves this with two brilliant ideas: composability (breaking the UI into small reusable pieces) and the Virtual DOM (React calculates the minimal changes to apply to the real DOM).

box.title: Key concept: Virtual DOM
box.body:
Analogy: imagine an architect drawing a modification plan before sending workers to the job site. The Virtual DOM is that plan: React calculates the changes there, then sends only the strictly necessary instructions to the real DOM.

Technically, React keeps a lightweight copy of the DOM in memory. When state changes, it compares the old and new Virtual DOM (diffing), then applies only the differences to the real DOM (reconciliation).

Common mistake: believing the Virtual DOM is always faster than direct manipulation. On very simple interfaces, React's overhead is unnecessary: it shines on complex, highly dynamic UIs.

items.title: 1.1: Create a React project with Vite
items.desc: Vite is the recommended modern starter for React because it starts in milliseconds (native ESM dev server) and rebuilds very quickly. Typical workflow: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react, then cd my-app, npm install, npm run dev. The local server (often http://localhost:5173) supports HMR: when you edit a component, the UI updates without reloading the entire page.

items.title: 1.2: Structure of a React project
items.desc: Three files structure the startup: index.html contains the root element (<div id="root">), main.jsx mounts React with ReactDOM.createRoot(...).render(...), and App.jsx holds the first UI component. The src/ folder hosts application code, public/ static assets, and package.json scripts and dependencies. Understanding this flow helps you know where to plug in routing, providers (auth/theme), global styles, and global state.

items.title: 1.3: JSX: JavaScript + HTML combined
items.desc: JSX is a declarative syntax that looks like HTML but compiles to JavaScript calls (React.createElement). You can inject expressions with {...}, call functions, format data, and compose multiple components. Key rules: use className (not class), htmlFor (not for), camelCase props (onClick, tabIndex), and return a single parent (or a fragment <>...</>).

items.title: 1.4: Conditional rendering & lists
items.desc: Conditional rendering uses JS expressions: condition && <Block /> to show only when true, or a ternary condition ? A : B to choose between two branches. For lists, iterate over an array with .map() and return one component per item. Each element needs a stable, unique key (preferably a business id) so React correctly identifies elements between renders and avoids visual/perf bugs (lost focus, inconsistent order, unnecessary re-renders).

box.title: Checkpoint: Lessons 11.1 & 11.2
box.body:
Q1: Why is Vite preferred over Create React App?
→ Vite uses the browser's native ESM modules: the server starts instantly and only bundles modified modules. CRA bundles the entire project before serving, which slows down as the codebase grows.

Q2: In which file do we mount React on the DOM, and with which method?
→ In main.jsx, via ReactDOM.createRoot(document.getElementById('root')).render(<App />).

sample.label: JSX: imperative vs declarative
sample.html: // ❌ BEFORE React: imperative DOM (Vanilla JS) const div = document.createElement('div') div.className = 'card' div.innerHTML = `<h1>Hello Ada!</h1><p>2 + 2 = 4</p>` document.body.appendChild(div) // we describe HOW to do it // ✅ AFTER React: declarative JSX const Greeting = () => { const firstName = "Ada" return ( <div className="card"> {/* className, never class */} <h1>Hello, {firstName}!</h1> {/* JS expression inside {} */} <p>2 + 2 = {2 + 2}</p> {/* expression evaluated at render time */} {firstName === "Ada" && <span>Code legend</span>} </div> ) // we describe WHAT WE WANT, React handles the rest }

box.title: Key concept: What JSX really becomes
box.body:
JSX is not magic: Babel/Vite transforms it into React.createElement() before it reaches the browser.

<h1 className="title">Hello</h1>
becomes:
React.createElement('h1', { className: 'title' }, 'Hello')

Understanding this transformation helps you decode JSX compilation errors and know why if or for cannot be used directly in JSX: they are statements, not expressions that return a value.

box.title: Most common JSX pitfalls
box.body:
1. class → className: class is a reserved JavaScript keyword. Using it in JSX causes an error (or a silent warning depending on the version).
2. All tags must be closed: <img />, <br />, <input />: JSX follows strict XML rules, unlike browser HTML.
3. Single root element: a component can return only one root node. Use <>...</> (Fragment) to avoid an unnecessary <div> in the DOM.
4. false, null, undefined render nothing: this is intentional, and it is what makes {condition && <El/>} safe.

sample.label: Anti-pattern: key={index} on a dynamic list
sample.html: // ❌ Anti-pattern: array index as key items.map((name, index) => <li key={index}>{name}</li> // ⚠ If the list is sorted, React reuses the wrong // DOM nodes → misaligned inputs, jumping state ) // ✅ Best practice: stable business identifier users.map(user => <li key={user.id}>{user.name}</li> // ✅ The id stays the same even if order changes )

box.title: Silent bug: key={index} on a dynamic list
box.body: Using the index as key works only if the list is static and never changes order. As soon as you add, remove, or sort items, React reuses the wrong DOM nodes: you get inputs whose content no longer matches the data, animations on the wrong element, or state that "jumps" from one item to another. This bug is often silent: no console error, just inexplicable behavior. Absolute rule: always use a stable business id.

box.title: Checkpoint: Lessons 11.3 & 11.4
box.body:
Q1: Why do we write className instead of class in JSX?
→ class is a reserved JavaScript keyword (ES6 class syntax). JSX compiles to plain JS, so className is required to avoid the syntax conflict.

Q2: What is the practical difference between {condition && <El/>} and {condition ? <A/> : <B/>}?
→ The first renders nothing when the condition is false (show/hide). The second always picks between two alternatives: if condition is false, it renders <B/>.

box.title: Best practice
box.body: Install React Developer Tools in your browser (Chrome/Firefox). It is the #1 tool for debugging your components, inspecting props, and viewing state in real time.

modules.title: Components & Props
modules.subtitle: The art of splitting a UI into reusable pieces and making them talk

contentBlocks.html: Components are React's LEGO bricks. Each component is a JavaScript function that returns JSX. Props are the data a parent passes to its child: they always flow from parent to child (unidirectional data flow).

items.title: 2.1: Creating and naming components
items.desc: Convention: always start with a capital letter (Button, not button). One component per file.

items.title: 2.2: Props — passing data
items.desc: Props are read-only. A component must never mutate its own props. You can pass any type: string, number, object, array, function, JSX component.

items.title: 2.3: The children prop
items.desc: Lets you build flexible container components like Layouts, Cards, Modals. One of React's most powerful patterns.

items.title: 2.4: Composition vs inheritance
items.desc: React strongly favors composition. You never inherit components. Composition is more flexible and readable.

contentBlocks.html: useEffect lets you run side effects (API calls, subscriptions, DOM work) after React has painted the component. Understanding the dependency array is essential to avoid bugs and infinite loops.

contentBlocks.text: Common trap: internal state that « leaks » between routes

contentBlocks.html: When React Router goes from /users/1 to /users/2, it does not unmount the <Profile> component — it only changes its useParams. Result: all internal state (form in progress, previous fetch data, active tab…) stays as-is. One of the most common bugs for beginners — and experienced devs too.

box.title: Concrete symptom
box.body: You submit a quiz on /module/m11. You navigate to /module/m12: the quiz already looks submitted with the old answers. You fill a form on /users/42: going to /users/43 keeps the previous data.

contentBlocks.html: The idiomatic fix: pass a key prop that depends on the resource id. When the key changes, React fully unmounts the old subtree and mounts a new one → every useState/useRef resets cleanly.

sample.label: Router pattern: key on the resource id

box.title: Mnemonic rule
box.body: If a stateful component depends on an id passed as a prop (or read via useParams), put a key on it. That is almost always what you want: clear isolation, zero state leak, zero « reset » useEffect.

contentBlocks.html: TypeScript adds a static typing layer to JavaScript. The compiler checks type consistency at compile time, which prevents a whole class of bugs in production. Everything valid in JS is valid in TS: you can gradually migrate an existing project by adding types over time.

box.title: Why TypeScript in 2026?
box.body: TypeScript has become the default language of the React ecosystem. Most modern libraries are written in TS or ship types. Mastering TS is no longer optional for a React developer who wants to work on serious projects.

items.title: 19.1: Primitive types & annotations
items.desc: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, any, unknown, never, void. Understand the difference between any (disables everything) and unknown (type-safe).

items.title: 19.2: Interfaces vs type aliases
items.desc: When to use one or the other. Pragmatic rule: interface for objects (extensible, supports declaration merging), type for unions, intersections, and utility types.

items.title: 19.3: Unions, intersections, literal types
items.desc: Combine types to express fine-grained variations. Literal types ('idle' | 'loading' | 'error') let you model simple, type-safe state machines.

items.title: 19.4: Generics
items.desc: Create reusable parameterized types. The foundation of modern libraries (Array<T>, Promise<T>, Map<K, V>).

modules.title: Next.js 14 (App Router)
modules.subtitle: Server Components, Server Actions, file-based routing

contentBlocks.html: Next.js is THE React framework for production. App Router (v13+) is a deep overhaul: you no longer build « React + pages » but extended React, with components that run on the server by default, native streaming via Suspense, and mutations with Server Actions.

items.title: 22.1: App Router & nested layouts
items.desc: Folder-based routing. Each folder in app/ = a segment. page.tsx, layout.tsx, loading.tsx, and error.tsx have conventional roles. Layouts nest and are persistent across navigations.

items.title: 22.2: Server Components vs Client Components
items.desc: By default: Server Component (zero JS on the client, direct database access). 'use client' to switch to a Client Component (hooks, listeners, state).

items.title: 22.3: Server Actions
items.desc: Mutate data on the server directly from a form or handler, without creating an API route. Transparent, progressively enhanced, type-safe.

items.title: 22.4: Streaming, Suspense & loading.tsx
items.desc: Show the UI progressively while Server Components load. loading.tsx provides the automatic Suspense fallback for a segment.

sample.label: Server Component + Server Action
sample.html: // app/posts/page.tsx : Server Component import { db } from "@/lib/db" async function createPost(formData: FormData) { "use server" await db.post.create({ data: { title: formData.get("title") as string }, }) } export default async function Page() { const posts = await db.post.findMany() // ← direct DB access return ( <> <form action={createPost}> <input name="title" /> <button>Publish</button> </form> <ul>{posts.map(p => <li key={p.id}>{p.title}</li>)}</ul> </> ) }

box.title: Common pitfall
box.body: A Server Component cannot import a file marked 'use client' and vice versa without rules. Rule to remember: a Server Component can render a Client Component as a child, but a Client Component cannot import a Server Component directly (it must receive it via children).

modules.title: Global state: Zustand, Redux, Jotai
modules.subtitle: Sharing state between distant components

contentBlocks.html: As an application grows, you run into prop drilling: passing props through 5 levels so a deep component receives a piece of state. Global stores exist for that. But beware: the modern rule is to separate client state from server state.

items.title: 23.1: Zustand — modern simplicity
items.desc: Minimal API, no required Provider, granular selectors to avoid re-renders. Became the default choice in 2026 for shared UI state.

items.title: 23.2: Redux Toolkit
items.desc: The historical standard. Verbose but traceable and well tooled (DevTools, middleware). Still relevant on large applications with multiple teams.

items.title: 23.3: TanStack Query for server state
items.desc: The most important architectural choice: do NOT put server data in Zustand/Redux. TanStack Query handles cache, refetch, invalidation, stale-while-revalidate. Your client store no longer has to orchestrate all of that.

sample.label: Zustand: minimal store
sample.html: import { create } from "zustand" type CartState = { items: { id: string; name: string; price: number }[] add: (item: CartState["items"][0]) => void remove: (id: string) => void } export const useCart = create<CartState>((set) => ({ items: [], add: (item) => set((s) => ({ items: [...s.items, item] })), remove: (id) => set((s) => ({ items: s.items.filter((i) => i.id !== id) })), })) // In a component const items = useCart((s) => s.items) // ← granular selector const add = useCart((s) => s.add)

modules.subtitle: NextAuth / Auth.js, sessions, JWT, OAuth

contentBlocks.html: Authentication is not something you improvise: security mistakes are costly. The modern React ecosystem relies on solid building blocks (Auth.js, Clerk, Lucia…) rather than reinventing everything.

items.title: 24.1: Modern auth models
items.desc: Server session (cookie + sessions table in DB) vs stateless JWT (self-contained token). Trade-offs: revocability vs scalability. OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect to delegate (« Sign in with Google »).

items.title: 24.2: NextAuth.js (Auth.js)
items.desc: The most popular integrated solution for Next.js. Ready-made OAuth providers, session management, customizable callbacks, DB integration via Prisma.

items.title: 24.3: Protected routes & middleware
items.desc: Verify authentication on the server (Next.js middleware) rather than on the client only. Middleware runs on the Edge, before the page is even rendered.

box.title: Security rules to memorize
box.body: 1) Never store a sensitive token in localStorage (XSS). 2) Always use httpOnly + Secure + SameSite=Lax cookies. 3) Authorization checks must always happen on the server — the client can lie.

modules.subtitle: Prisma, Drizzle, PostgreSQL

contentBlocks.html: A modern React developer frequently works with the database through a type-safe ORM. Choosing the right tool and understanding what it does under the hood avoids performance and migration disasters.

items.title: 25.1: PostgreSQL for front-end developers
items.desc: Essential concepts to master: schema, primary/foreign keys, indexes, joins, transactions. Know how to read an EXPLAIN and spot a missing index.

items.title: 25.2: Prisma — the modern ORM
items.desc: Declarative schema (schema.prisma), versioned migrations, auto-generated TypeScript client with perfect typing. Ideal for projects getting started.

items.title: 25.3: Drizzle — the type-safe alternative
items.desc: Closer to SQL, without a heavy abstract runtime, fantastic on the Edge. For those who want fine control over generated queries.

sample.html: // prisma/schema.prisma model User { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) email String @unique name String? posts Post[] } model Post { id Int @id @default(autoincrement()) title String author User @relation(fields: [authorId], references: [id]) authorId Int } // Usage in code const authors = await prisma.user.findMany({ include: { posts: true }, where: { posts: { some: {} } }, // users with at least one post }) // authors is fully typed: User & { posts: Post[] }

box.body: The N+1 problem: you iterate over a list and run a query per item. Result: 1 + N queries instead of one. Solution with Prisma: use include or select to preload relations. Always check the generated SQL in dev logs.

items.title: 26.1: Test pyramid
items.desc: Lots of fast unit and integration tests, a few e2e tests on critical paths. Avoid the « all e2e » anti-pattern: slow, flaky, and expensive to maintain.

items.desc: Test a component the way a user would use it: find by role/text, click, type, verify what appears. Never test internal state or private methods.

items.title: 26.3: Playwright for e2e tests

items.desc: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) < 2.5s ; INP (Interaction to Next Paint) < 200ms ; CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) < 0.1. The 3 metrics that define a good experience (and your SEO).

items.title: 27.2: next/image & lazy loading
items.desc: Automatic optimization: modern formats (AVIF/WebP), responsive with sizes, fixed dimensions to avoid CLS, native lazy-loading. One of the highest-ROI optimizations available for free.

contentBlocks.html: At this stage, understanding what happens under the hood becomes a real advantage: relevant optimizations, advanced debugging, and better intuition about React's behavior in pathological cases.

items.title: 30.1: The reconciler & Fiber algorithm
items.desc: Fiber splits rendering into interruptible work units. Each component → a Fiber node → attached in a tree. React can pause an in-progress render to handle an urgent interaction, then resume.

items.title: 30.2: Concurrent features
items.desc: startTransition / useTransition to mark an update as non-urgent. useDeferredValue to derive a value that can be « deferred ». Suspense for unified loading.

items.title: 30.3: Hydration & Server Components
items.desc: What happens between server HTML and the hydrated DOM. Server Components send an RSC payload (not just HTML), deserialized on the client. Understanding this clarifies EVERYTHING about the Next.js App Router.

sample.label: useTransition: prioritize interactions
sample.html: import { useState, useTransition } from "react" function SearchPage() { const [query, setQuery] = useState("") const [isPending, startTransition] = useTransition() const [results, setResults] = useState([]) function onChange(e) { const q = e.target.value setQuery(q) // urgent: keep the input reactive startTransition(() => { setResults(expensiveSearch(q)) // non-urgent }) } return ( <> <input value={query} onChange={onChange} /> {isPending && <span>...</span>} <Results items={results} /> </> ) }

exercises.instructions: Implement an ultra-simplified diff(prev, next) function that compares two node trees { type, props, children } and returns a list of operations (ADD, REMOVE, UPDATE_TEXT).
